general_topics.answer: The interesting part of AI red teaming is that you're not just trying to break a model—you are testing the interaction between its instructions, tools, context, and guardrails. A finding matters when it's reproducible, scoped, and tied to a real risk. Attacker creativity has to meet careful verification.

Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, lets a model look up relevant material from a chosen collection before it answers. The model can then ground a reply in retrieved passages instead of relying only on what it learned during training. The hard parts are usually retrieval quality, source freshness, and making it clear when the evidence is thin.

Threat modeling is a structured way to ask what you're protecting, who or what could threaten it, how an attack might work, and which controls matter most. A useful model stays tied to a real system and changes as the design changes; a long checklist detached from implementation quickly turns into paperwork.

Prompt injection is an attempt to make a language-model system treat untrusted input as instructions. It can arrive directly in a user's prompt or indirectly through documents, webpages, or tool results. The risk depends on what the model can access or do, so robust designs separate data from authority and keep sensitive actions behind explicit controls.
